proposals.officialTitle: Saginaw County Proposal 26-4 Saginaw County 9-1-1 Authority Millage Renewal Proposal

proposals.ballotLanguage:
Shall St. Charles Community Schools, Saginaw County, Michigan, borrow the sum of not to exceed Ten Million Four Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars ($10,475,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds therefore, in one or more series, for the purpose of:
remodeling, equipping and re-equipping, and furnishing and refurnishing school buildings; and preparing, developing, and improving sites?
The following is for informational purposes only:
The estimated millage that will be levied for the proposed bonds in 2027 is 1.34 mills ($1.34 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation). The maximum number of years the bonds of any series may be outstanding, exclusive of any refunding, is twenty (20) years. The estimated simple average annual millage anticipated to be required to retire this bond debt is 2.30 mills ($2.30 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation).
(Pursuant to State law, expenditure of bond proceeds must be audited and the proceeds cannot be used for repair or maintenance costs, teacher, administrator or employee salaries, or other operating expenses.)
proposals.officialTitle: St. Charles Community Schools Bond Proposal
proposals.yesVote: A YES vote authorizes the sale of $10.47 million in bonds, repaid through a property tax levy over the life of the bonds.

proposals.conservativeView: Bonds commit taxpayers to decades of debt service. Ask whether the project list is needs or wants, whether the district has maintained what it already has, and what the total interest cost will be. "No tax rate increase" often means extending an existing levy for many more years rather than letting it expire.
proposals.progressiveView: Bonds let communities fund major facility needs — safety, infrastructure, aging buildings — spreading the cost over the years the improvements will be used.

proposals.ballotLanguage:
Shall Hemlock Public School District, Saginaw and Midland Counties, Michigan, borrow the sum of not to exceed Seventeen Million Seven Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($17,750,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds therefore, in one or more series, for the purpose of:

The maximum number of years the bonds of any series may be outstanding, exclusive of any refunding, is twenty-seven (27) years. proposals.officialTitle: Hemlock Public School District Bond Proposal

proposals.progressiveView: Bonds let communities fund major facility needs — safety, infrastructure, aging buildings — spreading the cost over the years the improvements will be used.

proposals.description:

proposals.ballotLanguage:
Shall Breckenridge Community Schools, Gratiot, Midland and Saginaw Counties, Michigan, borrow the sum of not to exceed Twelve Million Four Hundred Thousand Dollars ($12,400,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds therefore, in one or more series, for the purpose of:
erecting, furnishing, and equipping structures and additions to the elementary school; remodeling, furnishing and refurnishing, and equipping and re-equipping school buildings, including HVAC and school security improvements; acquiring and installing instructional technology; and preparing, developing, equipping, and improving playgrounds, parking lots, and sites; and purchasing buses?

The maximum number of years the bonds of any series may be outstanding, exclusive of any refunding, is fifteen (15) years. The estimated simple average annual millage anticipated to be required to retire this bond debt is 2.22 mills ($2.22 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation).

proposals.ballotLanguage:
Shall St. Charles Community Schools, Saginaw County, Michigan, borrow the sum of not to exceed Ten Million Four Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars ($10,475,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds therefore, in one or more series, for the purpose of:
remodeling, equipping and re-equipping, and furnishing and refurnishing school buildings; and preparing, developing, and improving sites?
The following is for informational purposes only:
The estimated millage that will be levied for the proposed bonds in 2027 is 1.34 mills ($1.34 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation). The maximum number of years the bonds of any series may be outstanding, exclusive of any refunding, is twenty (20) years. The estimated simple average annual millage anticipated to be required to retire this bond debt is 2.30 mills ($2.30 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation).
(Pursuant to State law, expenditure of bond proceeds must be audited and the proceeds cannot be used for repair or maintenance costs, teacher, administrator or employee salaries, or other operating expenses.)
proposals.officialTitle: St. Charles Community Schools Bond Proposal
proposals.yesVote: A YES vote authorizes the sale of $10.47 million in bonds, repaid through a property tax levy over the life of the bonds.
proposals.noVote: A NO vote rejects the borrowing — no bonds are issued and no new debt levy is added.
proposals.conservativeView: Bonds commit taxpayers to decades of debt service. Ask whether the project list is needs or wants, whether the district has maintained what it already has, and what the total interest cost will be. "No tax rate increase" often means extending an existing levy for many more years rather than letting it expire.
proposals.progressiveView: Bonds let communities fund major facility needs — safety, infrastructure, aging buildings — spreading the cost over the years the improvements will be used.

proposals.name: Freeland Community School District Bond Proposal
proposals.description: $21.2 million bond (up to 20 years) for remodeling, equipment, site work and a stormwater project at the Learning Center playground.
proposals.ballotLanguage:
Shall Freeland Community School District, Saginaw, Midland and Bay Counties, Michigan, borrow the sum of not to exceed Twenty-One Million Two Hundred Thousand Dollars ($21,200,000) and issue its general obligation unlimited tax bonds therefore, in one or more series, for the purpose of:
remodeling school buildings and facilities; equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and refurnishing school buildings and facilities; and preparing, developing, improving and equipping structures, facilities, sites and a stormwater drainage project at the Freeland Learning Center playground?
The following is for informational purposes only:
The estimated millage that will be levied for the proposed bonds in 2027 is 1.984 mills ($1.984 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation). The maximum number of years the bonds of any series may be outstanding, exclusive of any refunding, is twenty (20) years. The estimated simple average annual millage anticipated to be required to retire this bond debt is 1.849 mills ($1.849 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation).
(Pursuant to State law, expenditure of bond proceeds must be audited and the proceeds cannot be used for repair or maintenance costs, teacher, administrator or employee salaries, or other operating expenses.)
proposals.officialTitle: Freeland Community School District Bond Proposal
proposals.yesVote: A YES vote authorizes the sale of $21.2 million in bonds, repaid through a property tax levy over the life of the bonds.
proposals.noVote: A NO vote rejects the borrowing — no bonds are issued and no new debt levy is added.
proposals.conservativeView: Bonds commit taxpayers to decades of debt service. Ask whether the project list is needs or wants, whether the district has maintained what it already has, and what the total interest cost will be. "No tax rate increase" often means extending an existing levy for many more years rather than letting it expire.
proposals.progressiveView: Bonds let communities fund major facility needs — safety, infrastructure, aging buildings — spreading the cost over the years the improvements will be used.
proposals.taxImpact: District says no net increase in the overall school tax rate — it will drop its sinking fund as the bond levy starts (1.98 mills in 2027).

proposals.name: Proposal 1 Proposed City Charter Amendment to Section 45
proposals.description: Removes the 1979 charter cap that limits city property-tax revenue to the dollar amount collected in 1978–79 ($3.83M), while keeping the 7.5-mill rate limit and 3-mill emergency provision. Effectively lets the city collect up to the full 7.5 mills.
proposals.ballotLanguage:
The present section limits the property tax rate to the lesser of 7.5 mills or that needed to yield the same revenue as was received in the 1978-1979 fiscal year ($3,828,778). It also provides for a temporary 3 mill additional tax for a declared emergency. The proposed amendment would eliminate the tax cap on the gross dollar amount of revenue that may be levied but otherwise maintains all other provisions, including the number of mills that may be levied.
Shall this proposal be adopted?
proposals.officialTitle: Proposal 1 Proposed City Charter Amendment to Section 45
proposals.yesVote: A YES vote approves a new levy of 7.5 mills — this is a tax increase.
proposals.noVote: A NO vote rejects the new tax; your property tax rate stays where it is.
proposals.conservativeView: Removing a revenue cap is a tax increase by another name — the city could collect far more without another vote.
proposals.progressiveView: The 1979 cap has frozen city revenue at 1970s levels while costs have tripled; the mill limit still protects taxpayers.

proposals.ballotLanguage:

(Pursuant to State law, expenditure of bond proceeds must be audited and the proceeds cannot be used for repair or maintenance costs, teacher, administrator or employee salaries, or other operating expenses.)
proposals.officialTitle: Hemlock Public School District Bond Proposal
proposals.yesVote: A YES vote authorizes the sale of $17.75 million in bonds, repaid through a property tax levy over the life of the bonds.
proposals.noVote: A NO vote rejects the borrowing — no bonds are issued and no new debt levy is added.
proposals.conservativeView: Bonds commit taxpayers to decades of debt service. "No tax rate increase" often means extending an existing levy for many more years rather than letting it expire.
proposals.progressiveView: Bonds let communities fund major facility needs — safety, infrastructure, aging buildings — spreading the cost over the years the improvements will be used.
